title: Alien vs. Predator
full_review:
Horror film fans have always loved a good monster mash. Hollywood heavyweight bouts have included "Frankenstein Meets the Wolfman" (1943), "King Kong vs. Godzilla" (1962) and, of a more recent vintage, "Freddy vs. Jason" (2003).

Add to the frightfest fight card "Alien vs. Predator" (20th Century Fox), a cross-pollinating of two popular sci-fi franchises which had been percolating in development offices for 10 years before making its way to the big screen. Unfortunately, it wasn't worth the wait.

In the film, a team of scientists and mercenaries (including Sanaa Lathan and Raoul Bova) are hired by a billionaire industrialist (Lance Henriksen, who also appeared in the 1986 "Alien" sequel "Aliens") to explore a mysterious ancient pyramid which is discovered buried far beneath the Antarctic ice cap.

Once there, the expedition members find themselves live bait in a battle royal between the two eponymous space species sparring for bragging rights in the galaxy.

As directed by Paul W.S. Anderson, the film has some moments, its eerie Antarctic atmospherics echoing the 1951 black-and-white sci-fi classic "The Thing." But for the most part, the movie is devoid of substance or style, its repellent cavalcade of slimy special effects drowning out any real suspense.

"Alien vs. Predator" -- or "AVP" in billboard shorthand -- has plenty of oozing glow-in-the-dark blood, but very little in the way of story and three-dimensional characters, though its who-would-win-in-a-face-off conceit will probably appeal to its core comic-book and video-game audience and generate respectable box-office numbers. Not all the rib-busting is caused by the face-sucking alien larvae; some of it is the result of unintended fits of audience laughter, such as those erupting during a ridiculous extraterrestrial buddy-movie ending.

However, cast members manage to keep a straight face while going through the motions. But beyond getting the narrative ball rolling and supplying some occasional clarifying exposition, their only raison d'etre is to furnish the proceedings with warm-blooded moving targets to be picked off one by one, more often than not being impaled by the creepy critters' venomous tendrils. And while some scenes push the boundaries of the film's PG-13 rating, much of the carnage occurs off screen.

The original movies that spawned the separate franchises both worked because they had human rooting interests: Sigourney Weaver in Ridley Scott's 1979 "Alien" (with follow-up tours of duty in three sequels), and Arnold Schwarzenegger in John McTiernan's 1987 "Predator." Both Weaver's and Schwarzenegger's characters were well-developed. And while both films begat retread offspring, the first two "Alien" installments are considered classics of the sci-fi canon. The genre gene pool has thinned considerably in Anderson's movie, which lacks the inventiveness and intelligence of its iconic pedigree.

For fan and uninitiated alike, "Alien vs. Predator" may not make much sense and appear to be nothing more than two scaly, slithering space baddies slugging and sliming it out.

If you are thinking about shelling out cash to see this extraterrestrial tussle, just remember: Whoever wins, you lose -- your time and money, that is.

Due to gory action violence, an instance of rough language and scattered crude expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
